tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }

Roadmap item 0.3 is open as draft PR #49, stacked on #48: https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/49. All 676 tests pass, and clippy with `-D warnings` and `cargo deny` are clean.

- **Lints:** the workspace now denies `unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, `panic`, `dbg_macro`, `print_stdout`, `print_stderr`, `map_err_ignore`, `let_underscore_must_use` and `unused_must_use`.
- **Test exemptions:** unit tests are exempt through `.clippy.toml`. Integration tests, examples, benches and `fake_tsc` carry a file-level `#![allow]`.
- **Production code:** it had no `unwrap` or `expect` to fix. The 36 `let _ = …` discards became `.ok()` or a named binding, and one `map_err(|_| …)` got a named parameter.
- **CLI printing:** the CLI had 9 existing `println!` calls, so I allowed `print_stdout` there. I changed the `crates/cli/AGENTS.md` rule to match: command payloads go to stdout, and nothing uses `eprintln!`.
- **Dependencies:** `deny.toml` now has `yanked = "deny"`, `yoke-derive` moved from 0.8.3 to 0.8.4, and I removed the unused `pretty_assertions`.

I left `unsafe_code = forbid` for the non-binding crates out of this PR. It needs per-crate lint tables, so it's a separate change.

The stack is #48 (0.1), then #49 (0.3). The next item is 0.2 (architecture tests), which needs 0.1, then 0.4 (CI semver and MSRV), 0.5 (cache guards) and 0.6 (recall harness).

content.text:
Roadmap item 0.2 is open as draft PR #50, stacked on #49: https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/50. All 685 tests pass, which is nine new ones, and clippy is clean.

`crates/core/tests/architecture.rs` pins six rules by scanning production source (comments and `cfg(test)` items are skipped):
- **Extractor and `known.rs`:** neither imports the resolver or pipeline.
- **Resolver:** it imports the pipeline only in `resolver/extends.rs` and `resolver/mod.rs`. Item 2.3 removes those and deletes the allowlist entries.
- **`OpaqueDetail::new`:** only `known.rs`, `resolver/named.rs` and `types/output.rs` call it.
- **`types/output.rs`:** no `HashMap`.
- **Extractor signatures:** no public one exposes an OXC type.
- **Manifests:** none sets `panic = "abort"`.

Each rule has a negative test showing it fires. Every allowlist entry carries a reason and fails the test if it goes stale.

The roadmap said `OpaqueDetail::new` should appear only in `known.rs` and deserialization. The resolver's depth guard in `resolver/named.rs` also builds one, so I allowlisted it with a reason. That's a candidate for a typed constructor later.

The stack is now #48, #49, #50. Next I'll do 0.4 (CI semver-checks and MSRV), then 0.5 (cache guards) and 0.6 (recall harness).

# Dependency updates. Every ecosystem is grouped into a single routine PR per
# week so the queue stays reviewable, with security updates kept in their own
# group so an advisory fix is never hidden inside a large routine bump.
#
# `cooldown` deliberately lags fresh releases: this repo pins GitHub Actions
# by commit SHA, and a week is long enough for a yanked crate or a pulled
# action release to surface before it lands in a PR here.
version: 2

updates:
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    open-pull-requests-limit: 3
    groups:
      routine-actions:
        applies-to: version-updates
        patterns: ["*"]
      security-actions:
        applies-to: security-updates
        patterns: ["*"]

  - package-ecosystem: cargo
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    open-pull-requests-limit: 5
    groups:
      # The oxc_* crates are released in lockstep and their minor releases
      # carry breaking API changes; keeping them in one PR means the
      # extractor and resolver are updated together or not at all.
      oxc:
        applies-to: version-updates
        patterns: ["oxc_*"]
      routine-cargo:
        applies-to: version-updates
        patterns: ["*"]
        exclude-patterns: ["oxc_*"]
      security-cargo:
        applies-to: security-updates
        patterns: ["*"]

  - package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    open-pull-requests-limit: 3
    groups:
      routine-npm:
        applies-to: version-updates
        patterns: ["*"]
      security-npm:
        applies-to: security-updates
        patterns: ["*"]

Components built by a wrapper call whose props travel as a type argument are now detected, for example `const Button = polymorphicFactory<ButtonFactory>(...)` where `ButtonFactory` is `Factory<{ props: ButtonProps }>`, or `const Item = withContext<HTMLDivElement, ItemProps>("div")`. p.write_text(s)
EOF

import * as React from "react";
import { MantineColor, MantineRadius, MantineSize, StylesApiProps } from "./Button";

/**
 * Mantine — @mantine/core TextInput
 *
 * TextInput composes two internal Mantine abstractions:
 *   1. `InputWrapperBaseProps` — manages label, description, error, and asterisk
 *   2. `InputBaseProps` — manages the visual input shell (sections, radius, etc.)
 *
 * Native `<input>` HTML attributes are passed through directly.
 *
 * Key patterns shown here:
 *   - `inputWrapperOrder` controls the DOM ordering of label/input/description/error
 *   - `leftSection` / `rightSection` render adornments inside the input shell
 *   - `leftSectionPointerEvents` / `rightSectionPointerEvents` control interaction
 *   - `withAsterisk` adds a required asterisk without setting `required` on the input
 *   - `wrapperProps` passes arbitrary props to the wrapping `<div>`
 *   - `styles`, `classNames`, `unstyled` from Styles API for deep customisation
 */

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Styles API slot names for TextInput
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/** The slot names exposed by Mantine's TextInput / Input Styles API. */
export type TextInputStylesNames =
  | "root"
  | "wrapper"
  | "input"

| Source | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| \`extends Pick<Gen<number>, \"x\">\` | \`x\` dropped, no warning | \`x\` kept |
| \`extends Omit<Base, keyof Other>\` | nothing omitted | \`Other\`'s keys omitted |
| \`props: Pick<Gen<number>, \"x\">\` | no props | \`x\` |
| \`props: Omit<Base, keyof Other>\` | nothing omitted | \`Other\`'s keys omitted |

Cause: step 0.5 of \`resolve_props_chain\` refused any base containing \`<\` (\"raw type_args can't represent nested generics\") and never read \`keyof\`. 4. **A `docgen.config.ts` that exists but fails to load is a hard error, not a silent fallback to defaults.** `try_load_config` (`config.rs:112-177`) surfaces node/tsx's real stderr on evaluation failure, and `into_pipeline_options` (`config.rs:33`) rejects unknown fields (`deny_unknown_fields`) and unrecognized `reactVersion` strings by name rather than defaulting. This is AGENTS.md non-negotiable #6 ("never fail silently") applied at the config layer: a config the user explicitly wrote getting quietly ignored due to a typo would be a plausible-looking but wrong result forever, and the regres
---
**Invariant 2: `reactVersion` never silently defaults.** `TryFrom<JsExtractOptions> for PipelineOptions` (`lib.rs:59-119`) treats every `Option<T>` field as "use `PipelineOptions::default()`" when `None`, _except_ `react_version`, which goes through `caliper_docgen_core::react_types::parse_react_version(v)` and hard-errors, naming the bad value, if the caller (e.g. via a TypeScript `as any` cast bypassing the `'react18' | 'react19'` `ts_type`) passes something that isn't one of the two accepted strings. This is a deliberate application of AGENTS.md non-negotiable #6 ("never fail silently") at the boundary where TypeScript's type system stops being a real guarantee.
---
`JsExtractOptions` (`lib.rs:34-55`) is deliberately flat — every field is a primitive, `String`, `Vec<String>`, or `Option` thereof, with two fields (`extra_paths_json`, `known_type_overrides_json`) pushed out to raw JSON strings specifically to dodge napi's object-marshalling complexity for nested maps. `TryFrom<JsExtractOptions> for PipelineOptions` (`Error = String`, not a structured error type) is the single place this flat shape gets reinflated into the richer `PipelineOptions` that `pipeline::extract`/`WatchSession` actually consume. Every one of the five entry points calls this same `TryFrom` before doing anything else — there is no code path that constructs a `PipelineOptions` from `
---
`ReactVersion::ref_as_prop`/`implicit_children` (`react_types.rs`) exist as fields, are correctly plumbed from the `--react-version`/`docgen.config.ts` CLI surface down to `PipelineOptions.react_version` (tested), and are then never read by anything in `crates/core`. That looked like a real gap — the original spec's worry was that `function Button({ ref, ...props }: ButtonProps)` (React 19's plain-prop `ref`, no `forwardRef`) wouldn't be recognized.

gh pr create --base test/declaration-shapes --head fix/nested-generic-props-args --title "fix: generic interface arguments and import-then-export barrels (roadmap 3.3 partial, RC3 and RC4, D1)" --body "Stacked on #68. Two root causes from the research, each reproduced by a failing test first.

**Generic interface arguments (RC3).** \`resolve_interface_chain\` ignored its \`type_args\`, so \`Box<string>\` left \`value: T\`. It now builds a substitution from the interface's declared parameters, applies it to the members, and rewrites the type arguments of its own \`extends\` clause (identifier-token substitution, so \`extends Box<T[]>\` becomes \`Box<boolean[]>\`). A \`parse_type_text\` helper (unions, intersections, arrays, literals, primitives, generic references; bracket and quote aware) rebuilds the stringified arguments; it replaces the narrower \`raw_arg_to_collected_type\` and stands in until item 2.1 structures them. The Mantine fixture now expands \`Record<Selectors, string>\` to the real slot-name union.

**Import-then-export barrels (RC4).** \`import type { X } from './x'; export type { X };\` was recorded as a local declaration, so no chain existed to follow. \`finish()\` now turns an \`export { local as exported }\` whose \`local\` is an import binding into the same \`ReExportNamed\` that \`export … from\` produces. This is the barrel style Mantine's core uses throughout; \`Anchor\` lost all of \`TextProps\` before.

**Ordering fix from review of my own earlier change:** \`ExtendsRef::Imported\` now keeps the extending interface's file as the consuming file when the name has an import binding, because the extends type arguments were written there; only an unbound name falls back to the recorded specifier. Passing the declaring file made the arguments resolve in the wrong file (the Mantine snapshot caught it).

Measured against react-docgen-typescript on the five mirrored corpora (share of its own props that Caliper reports):

| Project | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| mantine | 87% | 92% |
| chakra | 85% | 85% |
| antd | 95% | 95% |
| shadcn | 94% | 94% |
| spectrum | 97% | 97% |

The remaining Mantine gap is \`component\` and \`renderRoot\` on 220 polymorphic components: props a polymorphic callee adds, which need the callee's return type (roadmap Phase 4).

Two shape cases added to \`tests/shapes.rs\`. Verified: 701 tests pass, clippy clean, one snapshot changed (the Mantine fixture, for the better).

https://claude.ai/code/REDACTED"

{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"PreToolUse","permissionDecisionReason":"RTK auto-rewrite","updatedInput":{"command":"rtk gh pr create --base test/declaration-shapes --head fix/nested-generic-props-args --title "fix: generic interface arguments and import-then-export barrels (roadmap 3.3 partial, RC3 and RC4, D1)" --body "Stacked on #68. Two root causes from the research, each reproduced by a failing test first.

**Generic interface arguments (RC3).** \`resolve_interface_chain\` ignored its \`type_args\`, so \`Box<string>\` left \`value: T\`. It now builds a substitution from the interface's declared parameters, applies it to the members, and rewrites the type arguments of its own \`extends\` clause (identifier-token substitution, so \`extends Box<T[]>\` becomes \`Box<boolean[]>\`). A \`parse_type_text\` helper (unions, intersections, arrays, literals, primitives, generic references; bracket and quote aware) rebuilds the stringified arguments; it replaces the narrower \`raw_arg_to_collected_type\` and stands in until item 2.1 structures them. The Mantine fixture now expands \`Record<Selectors, string>\` to the real slot-name union.

**Import-then-export barrels (RC4).** \`import type { X } from './x'; export type { X };\` was recorded as a local declaration, so no chain existed to follow. \`finish()\` now turns an \`export { local as exported }\` whose \`local\` is an import binding into the same \`ReExportNamed\` that \`export … from\` produces. This is the barrel style Mantine's core uses throughout; \`Anchor\` lost all of \`TextProps\` before.

**Ordering fix from review of my own earlier change:** \`ExtendsRef::Imported\` now keeps the extending interface's file as the consuming file when the name has an import binding, because the extends type arguments were written there; only an unbound name falls back to the recorded specifier. Passing the declaring file made the arguments resolve in the wrong file (the Mantine snapshot caught it).

Measured against react-docgen-typescript on the five mirrored corpora (share of its own props that Caliper reports):

| Project | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| mantine | 87% | 92% |
| chakra | 85% | 85% |
| antd | 95% | 95% |
| shadcn | 94% | 94% |
| spectrum | 97% | 97% |

The remaining Mantine gap is \`component\` and \`renderRoot\` on 220 polymorphic components: props a polymorphic callee adds, which need the callee's return type (roadmap Phase 4).

Two shape cases added to \`tests/shapes.rs\`. Verified: 701 tests pass, clippy clean, one snapshot changed (the Mantine fixture, for the better).

https://claude.ai/code/REDACTED""}}}

# Architecture Decision Records

Short, dated records of _architectural_ decisions — ones that shape system structure, boundaries, or contracts other code depends on. Not a changelog, not a design doc, not a place to explain what the code does — comments and `ARCHITECTURE.md` already do that.

## Index

One line per ADR, with what it guards. Add a line when you add an ADR.

- [1. Parse with OXC instead of the TypeScript compiler](0001-oxc-over-typescript-compiler.md) — do not add a type-checking pass to the default path. The opt-in backend is 0006.
- [2. Hand-write Serialize/Deserialize for PropType instead of deriving it](0002-manual-serialize-for-prop-type.md) — do not derive them on `PropType` or `CollectedType`.
- [3. Cache the DTS parse cache with positional (not named) MessagePack](0003-positional-msgpack-cache-encoding.md) — do not reorder, insert or remove `SourceData` fields without bumping `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION`.
- [4. Defer full type-checker integration](0004-defer-type-checker-integration.md) — superseded by 0006.
- [5. Contain panics at a single, per-item boundary](0005-panic-containment-boundary.md) — route anything reachable from a rayon `.map()`, a `DocgenPlugin` hook or a NAPI entry point through `contain_panic`.
- [6. Run the TypeScript backend as a second resolver](0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md) — do not patch `Opaque` leaves, give `crates/core` a compiler process or I/O, or route the backend through NAPI.

Changing any of these needs a new ADR.

## When to write one

Two gates, both required:

1. **Architectural.** It affects one of: system structure (module/crate boundaries, how components interact), a dependency or technology choice that ripples across the codebase, a data format or contract other code depends on, or a cross-cutting constraint (performance model, correctness discipline, security model).
2. **Expensive to reverse and not obvious from the code.** If it gets reverted in a year, what breaks, and would anyone know why?

If either answer is no, it's not an ADR.

Good candidates:

- Choosing OXC over the TypeScript compiler — a technology choice that shapes the whole extraction pipeline
- A serialization format with a hidden constraint (msgpack's positional encoding) — a data contract other code depends on
- Dropping a dependency, or an approach that was tried and abandoned

Not ADR material:

- A single function's algorithm choice, confined to that function — that's a code comment
- A bug fix — commit message, and if it's the kind of thing that could recur, a line in `rdt-coverage.md`
- A behavior-preserving refactor — commit message is enough
- A naming or style convention — that's `AGENTS.md` or a lint rule
- Anything already obvious from the code or from `AGENTS.md`'s non-negotiables
- Per-user preferences, workflow notes and tool quirks — that's agent memory

## Format

One file per decision: `docs/adr/NNNN-short-title.md`, numbered sequentially, never reused. Copy `0000-template.md` to start.

- **Never edit history.** If a decision changes, write a new ADR and mark the old one's status `Superseded by 000X`. Don't rewrite the old file to look like you knew all along.
- **Status** is one of: `Accepted`, `Superseded by NNNN`, `Deprecated`.
- Keep it short. If the technical depth doesn't fit on a screen, split it into its own doc and link it — see `0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md` pointing at `type-checker-integration.md` instead of inlining it.

## Writing it

Write like you're explaining it to the next engineer over their shoulder, not presenting it to a committee. Don't hard-wrap paragraphs at a fixed column — one line per paragraph, let the editor soft-wrap. Every other doc in this repo already does this; hard-wrapping just makes future diffs noisy when a sentence gets edited.

**Cut the filler.** If a sentence still means the same thing without a word, delete the word.

| Instead of | Write |
| --- | --- |
| "It's worth noting that this decision was made in order to leverage OXC's robust parsing capabilities" | "OXC parses in parallel with no type-checking pass" |
| "This represents a significant improvement in performance" | "32ms instead of several seconds" |
| "We decided to essentially utilize a positional encoding approach" | "We use positional encoding" |

# 0006. Run the TypeScript backend as a second resolver, not a leaf patcher

**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-09-26

## Context

The structural resolver can't substitute generics through alias chains or evaluate conditional and mapped types. Ten components account for 2,696 of the 2,720 props missing against react-docgen-typescript (RDT) in the 2026-07-25 baseline (`docs/benchmarks.md`). ADR 0004 deferred a fix until TypeScript 7 offered a usable route.

TypeScript 7.0 has no programmatic API. 7.1 adds one, available now as `tsc --api` in `typescript@next`. RDT's own algorithm runs on it and returned exactly RDT's props on 13 components (`docs/type-checker-integration.md`).

## Decision

Add an opt-in semantic resolver that runs RDT's algorithm on `tsc --api` and merges its result into the structural one per component. Structural stays the default and the fallback.

- `crates/core` defines an owned-data semantic result and does the merge. It stays free of I/O.
- A feature-gated crate spawns `tsc --api`, speaks its protocol and owns the process. Rust spawns it, in the CLI and the NAPI addon alike. The JS client is not involved.
- We pin an exact `typescript` build and check its version at startup, because the protocol has no version handshake.

## Consequences

- Components the structural resolver can't finish get RDT's prop set without a new heuristic per gap.
- The API is `typescript/unstable/*` and still changing. Pinning limits the damage, but a 7.1 change can force rework.
- The backend costs a process per run, so it is off by default.
- Users need `typescript` 7.1 or later. Without it, extraction still succeeds and emits a diagnostic.
- tsc sees a dependency edit only when told, so `WatchSession::update_file` must notify it, with a parity test against `extract()`.
- Checker types don't fit `PropType` losslessly, and `ExtractionOutput` has no schema version. A follow-up ADR decides the representation.

## Alternatives considered

- **Replace `Opaque` leaves with tsc answers** (ADR 0004's model). `OpaqueDetail` holds only a raw string and a reason, and can't be built or inspected outside `crates/core`. Some types resolve to `Named` on purpose with no diagnostic (bare generic parameters, TypeScript utility types), so no leaf marks them.
- **Call the JS client through NAPI.** The CLI is a standalone binary that uses Node only to load `docgen.config.ts`, the binding never calls into JS, and the resolver is synchronous rayon code.
- **Node sidecar**, as `config.rs` does for `docgen.config.ts`. It adds a process hop and a Node dependency. It is the fallback if protocol churn outpaces a Rust client.
- **Vendor typescript-go internals**, as tsgolint does. The repo was closed on 2026-08-20 and the API is the supported surface.
- **TypeScript 7 LSP.** Not evaluated further, because the API exposes each query the algorithm needs directly.

77:| Where | `microsoft/TypeScript` `main` (`7.1.0-dev`). typescript-go closed on 2026-08-20 |
80:| Launch | `tsc --api --async --cwd <dir>`: JSON-RPC with LSP-style `Content-Length` framing, handled concurrently. Without `--async`: msgpack over stdio, strictly serial. `--pipe` uses a socket |
81:| Stability | JS entry points are `typescript/unstable/*`. The protocol has no version handshake, so pin the build |
97:Method: RDT 2.4.0 on typescript@6.0.3 (`apps/validate`'s RDT is pinned to a TS6 API — see "The RDT oracle" below) with the harness options (`shouldExtractLiteralValuesFromEnum`, `shouldRemoveUndefinedFromOptional`, `propFilter: { skipPropsWithoutDoc: false }`), against the algorithm above via `apps/validate/src/run-semantic.ts` on typescript@next. 114:- Most are non-component exports the "single-parameter function" heuristic sweeps in — plain string-returning helpers (`antd/buttonHelpers.ts`, `headlessui/render.ts`'s `mergeProps`, `blueprint/blueprintTypes.ts`) whose "props" are `String.prototype`/`Array.prototype` members. RDT is equally permissive and picks these up too, so both tools agree these aren't components; the mismatches are TS 6 vs TS 7.1-dev lib.d.ts differences (e.g. `padStart`'s parameter renamed `maxLength`→`targetLength`) and per-run `Symbol.iterator` id suffixes, not a resolver bug.
146:- **Backend crate** (feature-gated, off by default) spawns `tsc --api`, speaks the protocol, and handles timeouts and supervision. `config.rs` has none of these today.
157:| Lifecycle | Client built and tested against a fake tsc and the real nightly (`crates/tsc-client`): missing binary, unsupported version, timeout, crash, restart storm, malformed or oversized frame, partial project failure, shutdown reaping, stale notification. Open: header-size cap, stderr that isn't UTF-8, honoring `handshake_timeout`, recovery after the restart cap trips, whether a restarted request may replay |
164:`apps/validate` depends on `typescript@next` directly (for `run-semantic.ts`'s own `tsc --api` probe), but RDT 2.4.0 crashes on import against it (`ts.JsxEmit` is undefined). RDT now resolves its `typescript` peer to `typescript@6.0.3` instead, via the aliased `typescript-next` package dependency `run-semantic.ts` imports from — no pnpm override needed, since pnpm overrides don't reliably rewrite a peer dependency's resolution (tried `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s `overrides: { "react-docgen-typescript>typescript": ... }`; the lockfile recorded it but RDT kept resolving against whatever `typescript` apps/validate depended on directly).

use camino::Utf8PathBuf;

p.write_text('''# 0007. Let the backend discover components, always compile it in, and keep structural as the default

**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-10-21

## Context

ADR 0006 made the TypeScript backend a second resolver that finishes components the structural resolver already found. Detection by shape now covers 92 to 99% of the components react-docgen-typescript (RDT) reports on five large libraries (`docs/edge-cases.md`), and what is left is a call with no type argument (`lazy()`, `createIconLoader("x")`) or a prop a callee adds (Mantine's `component` and `renderRoot` on 220 components). Only the checker can answer those: it knows what the call returns. Separately, callisto's rule is no cargo features in shipped crates, which ADR 0006's "feature-gated crate" contradicts.

## Decision

- **Discovery.** The backend may add components the structural pass did not find, using RDT's rule: a declaration whose type has a call signature with a props-shaped first parameter. Each carries the rule that found it and merges into the structural output; on a clash the structural entry wins.
- **Always compiled, enabled at runtime.** `crates/tsc-client` is a normal dependency of the CLI and the NAPI addon, with no cargo feature. A runtime option turns it on and is off by default, so a run without it spawns nothing.
- **Structural stays the default and the fallback.** A missing, unsupported or crashing `tsc` leaves the structural result untouched and adds a diagnostic.
- **Trigger.** The backend runs only for components the structural pass marked incomplete (an opaque leaf, a wrapper call with no resolved props, a callee-added prop it cannot see) plus whole-project discovery when the option asks for it. It is never a silent default.
- **Output.** `ExtractionOutput` gains an additive `schemaVersion` so consumers can tell whether discovery was on. Existing fields keep their shape.

## Consequences

- Wrapper calls the structural pass cannot see become exact without a new heuristic per library.
- Every build pays for the client's dependencies. Users who never enable the backend pay nothing at runtime.
- The checker needs `typescript` 7.1 or later and sees a dependency edit only when told. `WatchSession::update_file` must notify it, with a parity test against `extract()`.
- Checker types do not fit `PropType` losslessly, so a checker answer is converted at the boundary and anything that does not fit stays opaque with a reason.
- Determinism needs a gate: a clean run and an incremental run must agree, measured on the five corpora with dependencies installed.
- Supersedes only the feature-gating bullet of ADR 0006. The rest of 0006 stands.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the backend a feature of a separate crate.** Matches ADR 0006 as written but breaks the no-features rule and makes the shipped binary vary by build.
- **Run it by default.** Costs a process per run on projects that structural detection already handles and makes output depend on a toolchain being installed.
- **Add one structural heuristic per remaining shape.** The remaining shapes need the callee's return type; a heuristic per library is what the shape-based detector was built to avoid.
''')

**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-10-21

## Context

ADR 0006 made the TypeScript backend a second resolver that finishes components the structural resolver already found. Detection by shape now covers 92 to 99% of the components react-docgen-typescript (RDT) reports on five large libraries (`docs/edge-cases.md`), and what is left is a call with no type argument (`lazy()`, `createIconLoader("x")`) or a prop a callee adds (Mantine's `component` and `renderRoot` on 220 components). Only the checker can answer those: it knows what the call returns. Separately, callisto's rule is no cargo features in shipped crates, which ADR 0006's "feature-gated crate" contradicts.

## Decision

- **Discovery.** The backend may add components the structural pass did not find, using RDT's rule: a declaration whose type has a call signature with a props-shaped first parameter. Each carries the rule that found it and merges into the structural output; on a clash the structural entry wins.
- **Always compiled, enabled at runtime.** `crates/tsc-client` is a normal dependency of the CLI and the NAPI addon, with no cargo feature. A runtime option turns it on and is off by default, so a run without it spawns nothing.

- **Trigger.** The backend runs only for components the structural pass marked incomplete (an opaque leaf, a wrapper call with no resolved props, a callee-added prop it cannot see) plus whole-project discovery when the option asks for it. It is never a silent default.

- Wrapper calls the structural pass cannot see become exact without a new heuristic per library.

- **Add one structural heuristic per remaining shape.** The remaining shapes need the callee's return type; a heuristic per library is what the shape-based detector was built to avoid.

Phases 0 and 1 are done apart from 0.7, and most of Phases 2 and 3 are done. The recall gaps from the benchmark are mostly closed. It is 19 open PRs in one stack, #52 to #70, plus #46, the 0.2.2 release PR, which is separate. CI is green on #52–#54 and #68; #66 and #69 have Lint, SemVer and MSRV passing with the Test jobs still running; #70 is still running.

**Recall against react-docgen-typescript** (five source-only mirrors, own props):

| Project | Components found, before | Components found, now | Its props reported, now |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Mantine | 29% | 93% | 92% |
| Chakra | 9% | 92% | 85% |
| Ant Design | 88% | 97% | 95% |
| shadcn/ui | 98% | 98% | 94% |
| react-spectrum | 98% | 99% | 97% |

- **Biggest fixes:** detecting wrapper calls by shape (`factory<XFactory>(...)`, `withContext<El, Props>(...)`) and following barrel re-exports. Two barrel bugs were behind most of the missing Mantine and Chakra props: `extends` through a barrel, and the `import { X }; export { X }` style.
- **Speed:** Mantine went from 45 ms to 143 ms because it now resolves 346 components instead of about 105. The other four got slightly faster.

**Defects D1–D9** are fixed, except D1 (see Open below). The fixes are:
- parenthesized and `!` wrappers
- same-name enums
- unreadable files
- overloaded diagnostic codes
- `Pick` and `Omit` with generic or `keyof` arguments
- watch mode drifting from `extract()`
- eight options that were accepted and never read

I deleted those eight options rather than wiring them, which is a breaking change under a minor changeset.

**Foundations** (sibling `tests.rs`, strict lints, architecture tests, SemVer and MSRV CI, a cache byte-layout guard, a per-shape recall test) are in. The declared MSRV of 1.94 never built; it is now 1.97. I added ADR 0007 and recorded that `typescript@7.1.0-beta` ships a public API (`typescript/sync`, `/async`, `/proto`) and works with the Rust client.

**Open:**
- **Cannot be fixed structurally** (needs the TypeScript checker): calls with no type argument (`lazy()`, `createIconLoader("x")`, 8 components), and props a callee adds (Mantine's `component` and `renderRoot` on 220 components). This is roadmap items 4.3 to 4.5, a large piece of work I did not start.
- **Not done:** structured type arguments (2.1) and the rest of the architecture refactors (2.3, 2.5, 2.7). A text parser stands in for the type-argument problem. Also not done: 3.5, 3.6, performance work, and the release and site tasks (yank the old crate, update the site page, user guides).
- **Left out on purpose:** no proptest or fuzz targets yet (the golden-bytes test covers the cache layout).

**Things to know:**
- **Wrapper detection is on by default.** The roadmap's D1 recommended gating it behind a flag. I measured about 96% precision on Mantine and drop any guess that resolves to no props. Say if you'd rather gate it.
- **SemVer job.** It would have failed every PR with an intended break. It now passes when a pending minor or major changeset covers the break, and fails otherwise. I re-stacked the whole chain once to put that fix at the base, and again after finding three lint issues of my own.
- **Merge order.** Merge #52 first and go upward in order, one at a time. Every PR in the stack sits on its predecessor, and each lists its base.

I haven't merged anything and there are no draft PRs. #46 (the 0.2.2 release) is separate and still yours to merge.

Codex this a quick review of our work and found many structural issues:



<pasted_content id="d5b8">
# Caliper v1 review

My release assessment: the project has a credible speed advantage and much better structural coverage than it had a week ago, but the current open stack is not yet a v1 quality gate. I would continue the staged releases in the roadmap (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/docs/projects/architecture-roadmap.md), while treating watch correctness, detection precision, and a reproducible RDT comparison as required evidence before calling the output dependable for v1.

I reviewed the 20 PRs merged since October 14, all 20 PRs open on October 21, the final stacked branch, architecture and ADRs, tests, CI, and release workflow. This was a code and CI review; I did not run a new local build or benchmark. The working tree already contains uncommitted changes, which I left untouched. Entire transcript search could not read its saved Keychain login, so the retrospective relies on commits, PRs, and repository documents.

## What the week accomplished

The merged work renamed and published the Caliper packages, changed package metadata and licensing, updated dependencies, separated large inline Rust test modules, added architecture tripwires, and tightened production lints. The open stack then addresses real defects: deterministic enum selection, unreadable files, diagnostic codes, generic Pick/Omit, barrel resolution, watch parity, and several missed component declaration shapes. These are substantive improvements, and CI is green across the dependent stack.

The measured direction is promising. The roadmap’s latest source-only comparison (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/docs/projects/architecture-roadmap.md) reports component recall against RDT of 93% for Mantine, 92% for Chakra, 97% for Ant Design, 98% for shadcn/ui, and 99% for react-spectrum after #69. Those numbers establish progress on recall in that sample. They do not yet establish precision, output equivalence with dependencies installed, or v1 reliability under incremental updates.

## Findings ranked for release

| Priority | Finding and evidence | Consequence and action |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | The new wrapper rule can emit non-components. #62 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/62) accepts a PascalCase binding when a generic call has a plausible first argument, including any string or identifier; it does not inspect the callee’s return type. A local interface or a type ending in Props is enough to select props (wrapper.rs, lines 43–55 and 105–120 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/extractor/wrapper.rs#L43-L120)). For example, a Button constant returned as a string by makeLabel<ButtonProps>("button") meets these conditions. | This can inflate recall and pollute consumer output. Before enabling this rule as a default v1 behavior, run the roadmap’s per-family, hand-labeled precision gate, add representative non-component calls, and prefer callee evidence where available. |
| P0 | Watch snapshots can combine different revisions. #67 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/67) repairs several parity bugs, but global, reverse dependencies, named types, components, and diagnostics still publish separately. update_file swaps global, then independently updates the other stores (watch.rs, lines 180–212 and 241–301 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L180-L301)); snapshot() reads them separately (lines 129–150 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L129-L150)). Concurrent updates can also load a global revision other than the one whose named-type index a call just patched. | HMR consumers can observe stale or mixed props and diagnostics. Implement the documented immutable WatchRevision publication model, then test concurrent old-or-new complete snapshots and clean/incremental equivalence. Serializing updates is a reasonable interim containment measure. |
| P1, confirmed by control flow | Initial watch diagnostics disappear from later snapshots. initialize() receives output from cold extraction and seeds component_cache, but never seeds self.diagnostics; snapshot() reads only that map plus enum diagnostics (watch.rs, lines 110–150 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L110-L150)). | A cold parse or I/O error is returned once and then absent from watch --out snapshots until an update replaces it. Add an exact initial-output versus snapshot diagnostic test and persist the cold diagnostics. |
| P1, confirmed by control flow | The Vite virtual module retains removed or renamed components. On HMR, the plugin only assigns updatedComponents into currentOutput.components; it has no removal path (index.ts, lines 175–184 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/packages/vite-plugin/src/index.ts#L175-L184)). Rust #67 evicts a changed file’s old cache keys, but the incremental payload does not convey those removals. | A renamed Card can leave Card beside Panel in the virtual module. Return removed keys or a file-scoped replacement and test rename, deletion, and a component that stops resolving. |
| P1, confirmed by control flow | A recorded wrapper candidate can vanish without a diagnostic. try_record_wrapper_call returns true, preventing the normal skip diagnostic. During promotion, select_wrapper_props returning None simply continues (wrapper.rs, lines 60–89 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/extractor/wrapper.rs#L60-L89)). | This breaks the project rule that degradation is diagnosed. Emit a positioned diagnostic for a rejected recorded candidate, with care to avoid flooding users with ordinary non-components. |
| P1, semantic defect | #69 substitutes generic parameter names inside quoted text. Its substitute_identifiers scans identifier characters without tracking TypeScript string literals (chain.rs in #69 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/69/files)). For interface Wrap<T> extends Pick<Base, "T">, substituting T = number also changes the key string "T" to "number". | This can select the wrong inherited props while appearing resolved. Substitute on CollectedType nodes, as the roadmap already calls for, or at minimum make the temporary parser quote-aware and add this exact regression. |
| P1, release evidence | The RDT advantage is not yet proved end to end. The new shape test (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/148bf3ab/crates/core/tests/shapes.rs) checks exact component and prop names on synthetic cases. It does not gate corpus precision, types, required flags, defaults, diagnostics, dependency-installed projects, or latency. just recall in the roadmap is not implemented. Existing benchmarks.md (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/c32772ff/docs/benchmarks.md) is dated July and reports different figures and old package names from the October README. | Make one versioned, reproducible scorecard for the five corpora: recall, precision, exact prop fields, degradations, wall time, peak memory, and clean/watch parity. State the hardware, dependency state, tool versions, and comparison mode beside every claim. |

### Architectural issues

1. The semantic model is still partly text. ComponentMapping and ExtendsRef carry type arguments as strings; #69 adds a parser that reconstructs unions, intersections, arrays, and generic references from display text. This improves cases now but preserves the failure class behind D1 and creates a second TypeScript grammar in the resolver. Complete roadmap item 2.1, Vec<CollectedType>, before building more wrapper and backend behavior on this path. #69 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/69)
2. Detection provenance is partial. #60 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/60) adds DetectionRule, but classification still uses a first-success Option chain and a later wrapper promotion pass (visit.rs, lines 229–261 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/extractor/visit.rs#L229-L261)). There is no common typed Detection { Component, Skip, NotCandidate } contract yet. That makes rule precedence, declined candidates, and diagnostics harder to reason about as more shapes are added.
3. ADR 0007 needs a precise merge contract. ADR 0007 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/docs/adr/0007-backend-discovers-components-and-compiles-in.md) says a structural entry wins on a discovery clash; ADR 0006 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/c32772ff/docs/adr/0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md) and the backend design say semantic props replace incomplete structural props. These can coexist only if “discovery clash” and “prop completion” are distinct operations. Define that distinction and its tests before wiring the backend. Likewise, schemaVersion should identify the output contract; use separate provenance to tell consumers which backend ran.
4. A layering back edge remains. The resolver still imports pipeline::HtmlAttributeMode (resolver/mod.rs, line 142 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/resolver/mod.rs#L142)), contrary to the stated crate/module direction and roadmap 2.3. Move resolver configuration into the shared types boundary before adding backend merge logic.
5. Watch performance lacks a current gate. Every update clones GlobalSourceData inside ArcSwap::rcu (watch.rs, lines 186–190 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L186-L190)), rebuilds reverse dependencies, and constructs a resolution context. It may be acceptable at today’s corpus size, but the claimed roughly 2 ms edit path needs measurement after the fixes and on large dependency-installed projects. Profile allocation and peak memory before changing data structures.

### Rust, security, and maintainability

- The stronger lint and architecture tests are good safeguards. I did not find evidence of a production unwrap() violation in the reviewed stack. There is a small consistency miss: an internal std::collections::HashMap remains in pipeline collection where project rules call for FxHashMap (pipeline/mod.rs, line 379 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/mod.rs#L379)).
- The tests added for watch parity compare components and enums in their visible() helper, omitting diagnostics (watch/tests.rs, lines 949–952 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch/tests.rs#L949-L952)). That omission is directly relevant to the initial-diagnostics defect.
- The real Vite/native integration tests are designed to skip when no locally built .node file exists. CI’s test-ts recipe runs the plugin unit suite; green CI therefore does not prove the real binding and plugin operate together on the release artifacts. Run those integration tests against a built native addon in at least one CI lane.
- I found no confirmed exploitable security vulnerability in this review. The exposed inputs still deserve a release-specific robustness gate: malformed TS, cache decoding, process framing, and package install behavior. The roadmap’s proposed property/fuzz work was deferred by #53 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/53); its golden cache layout test guards format changes, not arbitrary malformed data.
- Documentation drift is now a DX issue. docs/STATUS.md still says September and “fully tested”; the architecture notes still describe some already-fixed watch behavior; MIGRATING.md and docs/benchmarks.md retain the old name. A user comparing Caliper with RDT should encounter one current set of commands and claims.

## All outstanding PRs

The 18 PRs from #52 to #70 are a dependent stack, so their green checks validate each proposed head against its named parent branch; they are not 18 independently mergeable changes to main.

| PRs | Assessment |
|---|---|
| #52 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/52), #53 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/53), #54 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/54) | Useful foundations: MSRV/SemVer gate, cache byte guard, and parenthesis/non-null detection. #53 is narrower than the roadmap’s proposed property and fuzz gate. |
| #56 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/56), #57 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/57), #58 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/58) | Worth landing as correctness work: deterministic enums, I/O reporting, and clearer codes. Check cache-version and diagnostic compatibility together. |
| #59 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/59), #60 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/60), #61 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/61) | Builders and typed function detection reduce duplication and improve recall. Detection classification and provenance remain incomplete; add negative fixtures for PascalCase helpers. |
| #62 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/62) | Highest-risk new behavior in the stack. Require measured precision and the missing rejection diagnostic before making its output a v1 claim. |
| #63 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/63), #64 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/64), #65 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/65) | Barrel and utility-type work addresses real missing props; #64 records improved measurements. Re-run against installed dependencies and exact fields. #65 should ultimately share structured arguments with #69. |
| #66 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/66), #67 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/67), #68 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/68) | Removing dead options fixes misleading DX. #67 closes several known watch defects but does not establish coherent revision publication. #68 adds useful exact-name fixtures, not the proposed recall harness. |
| #69 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/69), #70 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/70) | #69 materially improves generic and barrel handling, with the string-substitution defect above. #70 records the backend direction; resolve merge precedence, trigger observability, and provenance before implementation. |
| #46 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/46) | Separate 0.2.2 release PR, with no PR checks shown. Its merge triggers the publish workflow. Review the exact package/version manifest and release run independently of the feature stack. |
| #44 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/44) | Separate Dependabot PR. CI is red: lint fails because five archived Markdown files fail oxfmt. Hold it until that check passes; the failure is formatting, not a Rust test failure. |

None of the open PRs showed a recorded review decision in the GitHub metadata I retrieved. All checks shown for #52–#70 were successful; that is useful evidence, but the missing product and concurrency gates above remain.

## Recommended v1 sequence

1. Land the correctness stack in order, with focused fixes for #69’s quoted-key substitution and #62’s rejected-candidate diagnostic and false-positive gate.
2. Make watch output coherent, then verify exact components, props, enums, diagnostics, rename/removal behavior, and concurrent snapshots against cold extraction. Include the Vite virtual module in that gate.
3. Publish a reproducible Caliper-versus-RDT scorecard. Lead with accuracy and precision at a stated mode, then speed and memory for the same projects. Keep the structural default and opt-in checker results separate.
4. Finish the type-argument and detection contracts before integrating the TypeScript backend. Settle ADR 0007’s merge and provenance rules first.
5. Run release-artifact tests and refresh user docs before labeling v1: native addon plus Vite integration, platform package installation, current CLI/API guides, and one maintained benchmark page.

Caliper’s strongest value proposition is already visible: fast structural extraction with useful diagnostics and incremental access. For v1, the decisive proof is that those advantages survive real library shapes, false-positive review, file edits, and packaged installation with results a user can reproduce.
</pasted_content id="d5b8">


I want you to vet these and look for similar patterns of issues. We might have a lot more. Be thorough and think like a principal engineer driving quality architecture, performance and DX

# crates/cli

Thin command layer — no extraction logic. Each command parses args and delegates to `caliper-docgen-core::pipeline`.

## Layout

```
main.rs              — Cli struct, Command enum, *Args structs, main(), init_tracing()
commands/            — one file per subcommand (extract, watch, inspect, check, completions)

# Caliper v1 review

My release assessment: the project has a credible speed advantage and much better structural coverage than it had a week ago, but the current open stack is not yet a v1 quality gate. I would continue the staged releases in the roadmap (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/docs/projects/architecture-roadmap.md), while treating watch correctness, detection precision, and a reproducible RDT comparison as required evidence before calling the output dependable for v1.

I reviewed the 20 PRs merged since October 14, all 20 PRs open on October 21, the final stacked branch, architecture and ADRs, tests, CI, and release workflow. This was a code and CI review; I did not run a new local build or benchmark. The working tree already contains uncommitted changes, which I left untouched. Entire transcript search could not read its saved Keychain login, so the retrospective relies on commits, PRs, and repository documents.

## What the week accomplished

The merged work renamed and published the Caliper packages, changed package metadata and licensing, updated dependencies, separated large inline Rust test modules, added architecture tripwires, and tightened production lints. The open stack then addresses real defects: deterministic enum selection, unreadable files, diagnostic codes, generic Pick/Omit, barrel resolution, watch parity, and several missed component declaration shapes. These are substantive improvements, and CI is green across the dependent stack.

The measured direction is promising. The roadmap’s latest source-only comparison (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/docs/projects/architecture-roadmap.md) reports component recall against RDT of 93% for Mantine, 92% for Chakra, 97% for Ant Design, 98% for shadcn/ui, and 99% for react-spectrum after #69. Those numbers establish progress on recall in that sample. They do not yet establish precision, output equivalence with dependencies installed, or v1 reliability under incremental updates.

## Findings ranked for release

| Priority | Finding and evidence | Consequence and action |
|---|---|---|
| P0 | The new wrapper rule can emit non-components. #62 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/62) accepts a PascalCase binding when a generic call has a plausible first argument, including any string or identifier; it does not inspect the callee’s return type. A local interface or a type ending in Props is enough to select props (wrapper.rs, lines 43–55 and 105–120 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/extractor/wrapper.rs#L43-L120)). For example, a Button constant returned as a string by makeLabel<ButtonProps>("button") meets these conditions. | This can inflate recall and pollute consumer output. Before enabling this rule as a default v1 behavior, run the roadmap’s per-family, hand-labeled precision gate, add representative non-component calls, and prefer callee evidence where available. |
| P0 | Watch snapshots can combine different revisions. #67 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/67) repairs several parity bugs, but global, reverse dependencies, named types, components, and diagnostics still publish separately. update_file swaps global, then independently updates the other stores (watch.rs, lines 180–212 and 241–301 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L180-L301)); snapshot() reads them separately (lines 129–150 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L129-L150)). Concurrent updates can also load a global revision other than the one whose named-type index a call just patched. | HMR consumers can observe stale or mixed props and diagnostics. Implement the documented immutable WatchRevision publication model, then test concurrent old-or-new complete snapshots and clean/incremental equivalence. Serializing updates is a reasonable interim containment measure. |
| P1, confirmed by control flow | Initial watch diagnostics disappear from later snapshots. initialize() receives output from cold extraction and seeds component_cache, but never seeds self.diagnostics; snapshot() reads only that map plus enum diagnostics (watch.rs, lines 110–150 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L110-L150)). | A cold parse or I/O error is returned once and then absent from watch --out snapshots until an update replaces it. Add an exact initial-output versus snapshot diagnostic test and persist the cold diagnostics. |
| P1, confirmed by control flow | The Vite virtual module retains removed or renamed components. On HMR, the plugin only assigns updatedComponents into currentOutput.components; it has no removal path (index.ts, lines 175–184 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/packages/vite-plugin/src/index.ts#L175-L184)). Rust #67 evicts a changed file’s old cache keys, but the incremental payload does not convey those removals. | A renamed Card can leave Card beside Panel in the virtual module. Return removed keys or a file-scoped replacement and test rename, deletion, and a component that stops resolving. |
| P1, confirmed by control flow | A recorded wrapper candidate can vanish without a diagnostic. try_record_wrapper_call returns true, preventing the normal skip diagnostic. During promotion, select_wrapper_props returning None simply continues (wrapper.rs, lines 60–89 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/extractor/wrapper.rs#L60-L89)). | This breaks the project rule that degradation is diagnosed. Emit a positioned diagnostic for a rejected recorded candidate, with care to avoid flooding users with ordinary non-components. |
| P1, semantic defect | #69 substitutes generic parameter names inside quoted text. Its substitute_identifiers scans identifier characters without tracking TypeScript string literals (chain.rs in #69 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/69/files)). For interface Wrap<T> extends Pick<Base, "T">, substituting T = number also changes the key string "T" to "number". | This can select the wrong inherited props while appearing resolved. Substitute on CollectedType nodes, as the roadmap already calls for, or at minimum make the temporary parser quote-aware and add this exact regression. |
| P1, release evidence | The RDT advantage is not yet proved end to end. The new shape test (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/148bf3ab/crates/core/tests/shapes.rs) checks exact component and prop names on synthetic cases. It does not gate corpus precision, types, required flags, defaults, diagnostics, dependency-installed projects, or latency. just recall in the roadmap is not implemented. Existing benchmarks.md (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/c32772ff/docs/benchmarks.md) is dated July and reports different figures and old package names from the October README. | Make one versioned, reproducible scorecard for the five corpora: recall, precision, exact prop fields, degradations, wall time, peak memory, and clean/watch parity. State the hardware, dependency state, tool versions, and comparison mode beside every claim. |

### Architectural issues

1. The semantic model is still partly text. ComponentMapping and ExtendsRef carry type arguments as strings; #69 adds a parser that reconstructs unions, intersections, arrays, and generic references from display text. This improves cases now but preserves the failure class behind D1 and creates a second TypeScript grammar in the resolver. Complete roadmap item 2.1, Vec<CollectedType>, before building more wrapper and backend behavior on this path. #69 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/69)
2. Detection provenance is partial. #60 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/pull/60) adds DetectionRule, but classification still uses a first-success Option chain and a later wrapper promotion pass (visit.rs, lines 229–261 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/extractor/visit.rs#L229-L261)). There is no common typed Detection { Component, Skip, NotCandidate } contract yet. That makes rule precedence, declined candidates, and diagnostics harder to reason about as more shapes are added.
3. ADR 0007 needs a precise merge contract. ADR 0007 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/docs/adr/0007-backend-discovers-components-and-compiles-in.md) says a structural entry wins on a discovery clash; ADR 0006 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/c32772ff/docs/adr/0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md) and the backend design say semantic props replace incomplete structural props. These can coexist only if “discovery clash” and “prop completion” are distinct operations. Define that distinction and its tests before wiring the backend. Likewise, schemaVersion should identify the output contract; use separate provenance to tell consumers which backend ran.
4. A layering back edge remains. The resolver still imports pipeline::HtmlAttributeMode (resolver/mod.rs, line 142 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/resolver/mod.rs#L142)), contrary to the stated crate/module direction and roadmap 2.3. Move resolver configuration into the shared types boundary before adding backend merge logic.
5. Watch performance lacks a current gate. Every update clones GlobalSourceData inside ArcSwap::rcu (watch.rs, lines 186–190 (https://github.com/orin-dx/caliper/blob/08bafb04/crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs#L186-L190)), rebuilds reverse dependencies, and constructs a resolution context. It may be acceptable at today’s corpus size, but the claimed roughly 2 ms edit path needs measurement after the fixes and on large dependency-installed projects. Profile allocation and peak memory before changing data structures.

### Rust, security, and maintainability

# Caliper v1 review

My release assessment: the project has a credible speed advantage and much better structural coverage than it had a week ago, but the current open stack is not yet a v1 quality gate. # crates/cli

Thin command layer — no extraction logic. Each command parses args and delegates to `caliper-docgen-core::pipeline`.

## Layout

```
main.rs              — Cli struct, Command enum, *Args structs, main(), init_tracing()
commands/            — one file per subcommand (extract, watch, inspect, check, completions)
config.rs            — docgen.config.ts loading, maps to PipelineOptions
output.rs            — comfy-table formatting helpers
```

## Rules

Command payloads go to stdout with `println!`; diagnostics, progress and everything on stderr go through `output.rs` or the tracing subscriber — never `eprintln!`. Error display uses `miette`. Progress uses `indicatif`.

Config loading (`config.rs`) runs the user's `docgen.config.ts` via node+tsx. The config file path is passed via env var, not embedded in a shell string — command injection risk otherwise.

input.description: Detection precision and silent drops
input.prompt:
You are auditing component detection in caliper-docgen, a Rust React prop extractor (OXC parse → per-file SourceData → GlobalSourceData → resolver → ExtractionOutput). Goal: find where detection admits non-components (false positives) and where it drops or declines input without a diagnostic. Think like a principal engineer preparing a v1 quality gate. Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/caliper/.claude/worktrees/release-0.2.0 (git worktree at commit 08bafb04). STRICTLY READ-ONLY: do not edit, stage, commit, stash, or switch branches, and do not run cargo (another process owns target/). For experiments use the prebuilt binary /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/review/caliper-docgen-08bafb04 with `extract --src --format canonical --json` (stdout JSON: components map with props, plus diagnostics). Put scratch projects under /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/review/detection/ (give each a package.json `{"name":"x","private":true}`). Read first: AGENTS.md, crates/core/AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/architecture/README.md and the extractor doc it links. Project rule: never fail silently — degrading must emit a Diagnostic. Code in scope: crates/core/src/extractor/ (visit.rs detector chain, component.rs, wrapper.rs, interface.rs, alias.rs, mod.rs finish()), and the pipeline step in crates/core/src/pipeline/mod.rs that drops wrapper guesses with no props. Do: 1. Build a realistic labeled corpus of PascalCase bindings that are NOT components but appear in real React codebases (styled-components/emotion `styled.div

`/`styled(Base)

`, createContext, Zod/Yup schemas, `createSlice<…>`, tRPC/redux/zustand stores, class instances, `as const` objects, generic helpers returning strings/objects, enums, icon maps, `lazy`, `memo` of non-components, factory functions returning config, `Object.freeze`, HOCs applied to non-components, typed PascalCase utility functions with an interface first param that return non-JSX, etc.) and run them. Report which are wrongly emitted as components, with the DetectionRule that admitted them where you can infer it. 2. Build realistic component shapes that are still missed or mis-propped, especially ones similar to shapes now supported (wrapper calls, typed arrows, forwardRef/memo variants, default exports, generic components `(props: P)`, components declared via `satisfies`, overloads, namespaces/compound components, `export default memo(...)`). 3. Find every path where a candidate is recorded/declined/filtered with no diagnostic (e.g. `continue`, `return None`, `else { return false }`), and say whether a user would reasonably need to know. 4. Check the existing detection tests (crates/core/src/extractor/tests.rs, crates/core/tests/shapes.rs) for gaps: do they assert content or only presence, and which negative families are missing. Report each finding as: title; severity (P0 = wrong output with no diagnostic, P1 = user-visible wrong or missing output with a diagnostic or likely in practice, P2 = maintainability); evidence (file:line); the minimal input and observed vs expected output from running it; confirmed (ran it) or suspected; and the general pattern it belongs to. Then give a short precision estimate per rule family from your corpus. Depth over breadth, no style nits. Keep the final report under ~900 words.

input.description: Text-level TypeScript handling
input.prompt:
You are auditing how caliper-docgen (a Rust React prop extractor: OXC parse → SourceData → GlobalSourceData → resolver → ExtractionOutput) handles TypeScript types as strings instead of structured nodes. Goal: find every place where type syntax is manipulated as text and inputs where that silently produces wrong props or types. Think like a principal engineer deciding whether the stringly-typed path can be trusted for v1.

Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/caliper/.claude/worktrees/release-0.2.0 (git worktree at commit 08bafb04). STRICTLY READ-ONLY: do not edit, stage, commit, stash, or switch branches, and do not run cargo (another process owns target/). For experiments use the prebuilt binary /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/review/caliper-docgen-08bafb04 with `extract --src <dir> --format canonical --json` (stdout JSON with components, props and each prop's structured `type`, plus diagnostics). Put scratch projects under /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/review/text-types/ (each with a package.json `{"name":"x","private":true}`).

Read first: AGENTS.md, crates/core/AGENTS.md, docs/architecture/README.md and the resolver doc it links, docs/adr/README.md. Known background: ComponentMapping.props_type_args and ExtendsRef type_args are Vec<String> display strings; roadmap item 2.1 plans Vec<CollectedType>.

Inventory, then attack, every text-level operation, including but not limited to: crates/core/src/resolver/collected.rs (parse_type_text, parse_generic_reference, split_top_level, the Raw fallback), resolver/chain.rs (substitute_identifiers, parse_string_union_keys, step 0.5 utility handling, React. prefix stripping), resolver/substitute.rs (raw_arg_to_collected_type, apply_generic_args), resolver/alias.rs, extractor code that stringifies type arguments (extract_type_name_from_type, extract_props_arg, classify_extends), CollectedType::to_raw_string round trips, scoped "file:name" key splitting, react_types html_element_from_type_arg, known.rs name matching.

Probe with realistic inputs: string-literal keys that equal a type parameter name (e.g. `interface W<T> extends Pick<Base, "T">`), template literal types, function types containing `=>` inside generics, `typeof x`, `keyof`, `readonly T[]`, tuples, object literal type arguments with `;`/`,`, nested generics with defaults, identifiers like Infinity/NaN, namespaces (`A.B<C>`), comments inside type args, conditional/indexed types, unions of generics, `React.X` vs `X`, Windows paths in keys. For each, run it and compare the emitted prop types against what TypeScript means.

Report each finding as: title; severity (P0 = wrong output with no diagnostic, P1 = wrong/missing output with a diagnostic or common in practice, P2 = maintainability); evidence (file:line); minimal input and observed vs expected (from running it); confirmed or suspected; the pattern. Finish with: a list of all text-level operations you found (file:line, purpose), which ones the planned structured type arguments would remove, and which would remain. Depth over breadth, no style nits, under ~900 words.

input.description: Incremental and parallel-path parity
input.prompt:
You are auditing whether caliper-docgen's incremental and alternate entry points produce the same results as a cold extraction, and whether they are safe under concurrency. Think like a principal engineer preparing a v1 gate for HMR/watch users.

Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/caliper/.claude/worktrees/release-0.2.0 (git worktree at commit 08bafb04). STRICTLY READ-ONLY: do not edit, stage, commit, stash, or switch branches, and do not run cargo or pnpm builds (another process owns target/). For experiments use the prebuilt CLI /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/review/caliper-docgen-08bafb04 (`extract --src <dir> --format canonical --json`; `watch --help` for the watch command and its --out option), with scratch projects under /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/review/parity/. You can drive `watch --out` in the background, edit files, and diff its output file against a cold `extract` of the same tree.

Read first: AGENTS.md (note its "sibling-path parity" and "assert content, not presence" rules), crates/core/AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/architecture/README.md, docs/architecture/pipeline-orchestration.md, docs/architecture/napi-binding.md.

Paths to compare: crates/core/src/pipeline/mod.rs (extract, extract_with_global, resolve_guarded), crates/core/src/pipeline/watch.rs (WatchSession initialize/update_file/snapshot), crates/binding/src/lib.rs (every NAPI entry point and its session registry), packages/vite-plugin/src/index.ts (virtual module, HMR handling), crates/cli/src/commands/watch.rs, and the LSP command if present (crates/cli/src/commands/lsp.rs).

Check, at least: components, props, enums, diagnostics (initial and after edits), stats; rename, deletion, creation of files and components; a component that stops resolving; files outside src dirs or excluded; edits to a dependency only (types file, barrel, re-export); cache interplay; how each consumer applies an IncrementalUpdate (do removals reach the Vite virtual module / watch --out?); publication of shared state (ArcSwap, DashMap, Mutex) — can a reader or a concurrent update observe a mix of revisions; ordering and determinism of the outputs; error/panic paths. Also review the watch tests (crates/core/src/pipeline/watch/tests.rs), binding tests and vite-plugin tests for comparisons that omit fields or assert presence only, and whether the real native-addon integration tests ever run in CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml, justfile).

Report each finding as: title; severity (P0 = wrong output with no diagnostic, P1 = user-visible wrong or stale output, P2 = maintainability/perf); evidence (file:line); minimal reproduction and observed vs expected (run it when the CLI can show it, otherwise state the control-flow argument precisely); confirmed or suspected; the pattern. End with a short recommendation for the publication model (what must be one atomic revision). Depth over breadth, no style nits, under ~900 words.

input.description: Determinism, cache, performance
input.prompt:
You are auditing caliper-docgen (Rust React prop extractor: OXC parse → SourceData → GlobalSourceData → rayon-parallel resolver → ExtractionOutput) for determinism, cache correctness, and performance. Speed is the product's main advantage over react-docgen-typescript, so treat regressions and unmeasured hot paths as real risk. Think like a principal engineer.

Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/caliper/.claude/worktrees/release-0.2.0 (git worktree at commit 08bafb04). STRICTLY READ-ONLY: do not edit, stage, commit, stash, or switch branches, and do not run cargo (another process owns target/). Use the prebuilt binary /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/review/caliper-docgen-08bafb04 (`extract --src <dir> --format canonical --json`, `--html-attributes full`, `--cache-dir <dir>`). Real corpora (untrusted third-party source, only read/extract them, never execute their code): /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/bench-inputs/{mantine,chakra,antd,shadcn,spectrum}. hyperfine and /usr/bin/time -l are available. Scratch space: /Users/gabe/.claude/jobs/ba6a68d6/tmp/review/perf/ (copy a corpus there if you need to mutate it).

Read first: AGENTS.md, crates/core/AGENTS.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/adr/0003-positional-msgpack-cache-encoding.md, docs/architecture/README.md.

Investigate:
1. Determinism: run each corpus several times (cold cache, warm cache, different cache dirs, a copy of the tree at a different path, and a copy with files touched in a different order) and diff full JSON outputs including diagnostics order. Find any FxHashMap/DashMap/rayon iteration order that leaks into output (crates/core/src/pipeline/, resolver/, extractor/, types/output.rs).
2. Cache correctness: crates/core/src/cache.rs — key/invalidation (mtime, size, content), what is cached (only .d.ts?), whether cached SourceData can be stale relative to code changes that don't bump CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION, concurrent runs sharing a cache dir, partial writes, corrupt or truncated cache files (try it), manifest handling.
3. Performance: time each corpus warm and cold, peak RSS; find hot-path costs in code (per-component clones of ResolveState / visited sets, GlobalSourceData clones in watch update_file, ReverseDeps rebuild per edit, O(n²) loops such as component-key disambiguation scanning a DashMap, repeated format!/String allocation in hot loops, repeated filesystem probes like canonicalize/resolver lookups per component, NamedTypeIndex rebuilds). Quantify where you can (e.g. scale a synthetic project to 2k/10k components and see how time grows).
4. Panic/robustness: malformed TS, deeply nested types, huge files, binary files with .tsx extension, symlink loops in src dirs.

Report each finding as: title; severity (P0 = nondeterministic or wrong output, P1 = measurable perf/robustness problem at realistic scale, P2 = likely problem not yet measured); evidence (file:line); reproduction and measurements; confirmed or suspected; the pattern. Include a small table of your timings (corpus, cold ms, warm ms, peak RSS MB, component count). Depth over breadth, no style nits, under ~900 words.

input.prompt:
You are auditing caliper-docgen's user-facing surface for a v1 release: documentation accuracy, CLI/API/plugin developer experience, and release/packaging risk. caliper-docgen extracts React component props from TypeScript (Rust core, CLI binary `caliper-docgen`, NAPI addon, Vite plugin, npm packages caliper-docgen / caliper-docgen-napi / caliper-docgen-vite-plugin, crates caliper-docgen-core / caliper-docgen / caliper-docgen-napi). It positions itself as a much faster react-docgen-typescript (RDT). Think like a principal engineer who owns DX.

finally:
